blocks.text: by @brandonmuskcy @Phaelon74
Reading KLD: What Those Nats Mean for Your Quant's Usability

More people now post KL divergence (KLD) numbers for low-bit quants. That is good, but many readers are not sure how the numbers map to real use, or how to measure them so someone else can reproduce them bit for bit.  In the following, we will explain KLD, give you an example through GLM 5.3 architecture and a general "rule of thumb" for what you can glean from KLD numbers at a glance (keeping it in the context described below).

KLD here is teacher-forced: the reference and the candidate read the same frozen token IDs, and at each position you compare their next-token distributions. The Distribution Fidelity Laws, written by Phaelon for the Local Inference Lab, use KL(reference || candidate) over the tokenizer's real vocabulary, averaged over every scored position [1]. A KLD number is evidence about one property. It does not measure free-running generation quality, benchmark accuracy, tool use, or behavior past the suite's context length [1].
Usability Tiers: Rules of Thumb

These tiers are not part of the laws. Law 10 says KLD has no absolute scale, that no threshold imported from another model, corpus, tokenizer, or serving stack carries a verdict, and that no fidelity number is a quality claim [1]. On the Index, Qwen's FP8 release of Qwen3.6-27B scores 0.016 nats and RedHatAI's FP8-dynamic gemma-4-26B-A4B-it scores 0.69. They come from different suites, so they cannot be ranked against each other [2].

As rules of thumb, the tiers follow how the llama.cpp community reads KLD. Its perplexity README lists LLaMA 3 8B on Wikitext-2 at 0.0014 nats for Q8_0, 0.031 for Q4_K_M, 0.10 for Q3_K_M, and 0.45 for Q2_K, and warns that its numbers are not directly comparable to other projects [3].

- Up to 0.05, Golden Zone: A normal user would not tell it apart from the BF16 weights in everyday use, but it is not identical. Q4_K_M (0.031) picks a different top token than FP16 at about 8% of positions [3].
- 0.05 to 0.10, Highly Stable: Small shifts, mostly on uncertain tokens. Coherent under standard testing.
- 0.10 to 0.15, Viable Boundary: Usable if sensitive tensors stay at high precision and you check the tails, long contexts, and your own tasks.
- 0.15 to 0.30, Noticeable Degradation: More factual slips, weaker instruction following, more format errors.
- Above 0.30, Trash Tier: At 0.50 most uses break. Q2_K (0.45) matches the FP16 top token only about 71% of the time [3].
A mean hides the tail. Law 9 requires the median, p90, p99, maximum, a depth profile, and top-1 agreement with every mean [1].
How Error Moves Through GLM-5.3

GLM-5.3 has 78 decoder blocks: 3 dense, then 75 MoE blocks with 256 routed experts, one shared expert, and top-8 routing [4]. Each FFN is gated: y = W_d(SiLU(W_g x) * W_u x), where * is the elementwise product. Each sublayer normalizes its input and adds its output to a residual stream; it does not replace the hidden state. A rounding error in one block becomes a small change in what that block adds, and later blocks add their own. Error compounds, but gradually. If it grew exponentially with depth, 4-bit quants of 60 to 90 layer models would not work. Error also spreads across positions through the KV cache, which is why Law 9 asks for a depth profile [1]. The routed experts hold most of the 753B weights, so in an expert-only quant nearly all of the error is FFN error at every KLD level.
What MoE Adds

Routing flips. Top-k routing is not smooth. If the 8th and 9th experts are nearly tied, a small upstream change can swap them, even with an unquantized router, because the router's input has shifted. Law 14 measures this with paired runs on the same tokens: QxQ uses the candidate's own routing, and BxQ forces in the reference's expert IDs while the candidate computes its own gate weights [1]. For Qwen's FP8 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, about 36% of (token, layer) routing choices differ from the reference, and forcing the reference's choices lowers mean KLD from 0.0173 to 0.0076 [2][9]. The laws call that gap a paired intervention result, not an additive decomposition [1].

Sparse attention. GLM-5.3's DSA indexer picks up to 2,048 earlier tokens per query [4]. That is a second top-k choice that can flip, and it only engages past 2,048 tokens. The Index's current suites use 2,048-token contexts [2][9], so they would not test it.
Cross terms. Holding the routing and combine weights fixed:
||Σ_e w_e·δy_e||² = Σ_e w_e²·||δy_e||² + Σ_(e≠j) w_e·w_j·<δy_e, δy_j>

With independent, zero-mean errors the cross terms average out. A systematic bias, such as a scale search that shrinks magnitudes, lines the errors up so they add. Measure it on calibration tokens instead of assuming it.
Mixed Precision, Not an FP8 RoPE Anchor

RoPE has no weights, weight quantization never touches it, and engines already run it in BF16 or FP32, so FP8 RoPE can only lower precision. Rotary precision does matter in the KV cache: DeepSeek's FP8 cache for MLA keeps the 64 rotary values in BF16 because they are sensitive to precision loss [5]. The laws pin the KV cache unquantized for scored runs (Law 2) and bind its dtype into the capture and the comparability key (Laws 5 and 10) [1].

What helps a borderline quant is quantizing the routed experts while keeping attention, the router, the shared expert, the dense layers, the embeddings, and the LM head at high precision. RadixArk's expert-only NVFP4 build of GLM-5.3 works this way [6]. The gain shows up as a lower KLD. It does not change what a given KLD means, so a claim that a 0.12-nat quant is fine in production needs task results (Law 10).
The Laws

LAWS.md is at version 15, has 17 laws, and is marked as a draft [1]. The pipeline refuses to publish an artifact that breaks one; where a law allows an override, it needs a named, recorded approval shown next to the numbers (Law 13). Four laws matter for anyone measuring KLD:
1. Zero baseline. The reference scored against its own capture must give exactly 0.0 on the same runner and tensor-parallel size.

2. Determinism. Eager only: no CUDA graphs, autotuning, or JIT kernel selection, prefix caching off, a fixed max_num_seqs, and identical settings for reference and candidate. The scorer also runs vLLM's batch-invariant mode, because most kernels change their numbers with batch composition [7][9].
3. Frozen input. Stored token IDs from a published suite, checked by SHA-256.
4. Real vocabulary. Score only the tokenizer's real vocabulary (kld_vocab_size). Padding rows make checkpoints incomparable.

The other thirteen cover binding and provenance (Laws 5, 6, 7, 12, 16), disclosure of head, tail, domain, and substitution effects (Laws 8, 9, 15, 17), and comparability, freezing, overrides, and routed models (Laws 10, 11, 13, 14) [1].
Replicate It

The leaderboard is at the Fidelity Index Hub [8]. The index dataset holds the one-pagers, and each reference model has an artifact repo with the suite, reference tensors, LM head, and receipts [2]. The tooling lives in the FidelityIndex branch of vLLM [9]. The install rebuilds one extension, the Marlin MoE kernel, patched for batch-invariant arithmetic so routed INT4, AWQ, and GPTQ candidates repeat bit for bit. Build it for your GPU's architecture only; Phaelon reports about half a minute.
Takeaway

Do not panic at 0.12 or 0.14 nats, and do not take it on faith. Check how it was measured and what came with it: tails, depth, domains, and for MoE models, QxQ and BxQ. Pair KLD with task results before calling a quant production-ready.  Local Inference Lab has great testing (that is not benchmaxxed on) such as our Hotel, Lavd, and Estonia Tests, along with Needle Tests, and various other benchmarks, and can give you a good idea if a quant is production ready.
